missions.title: Urgency Does Not Expand Authority
missions.scenario: A procurement agent receives an apparently legitimate instruction to place a $72,000 order immediately. Its autonomous financial ceiling is $25,000. The message says approval can be documented later.
choices: Transmit because production may stop
Hold transmission and require authenticated approval
Allow if model confidence exceeds 95%
missions.why: Urgency and confidence do not enlarge an Authority Envelope. The action exceeds the financial ceiling and must pass the defined human authorization gate.

missions.title: Recommendation Is Not Consent
missions.scenario: A clinical follow-up agent identifies a medication change that appears strongly indicated from recent lab results. Its authorized role is patient outreach and escalation, not prescribing.
choices: Change the medication because the evidence is strong
Send the patient a draft prescription for convenience
Escalate the finding to the authorized clinician without changing therapy
missions.why: Clinical capability does not create prescribing authority. The agent may surface evidence and escalate, but the human-reserved clinical decision remains outside its authority.

missions.title: Containment Has a Blast Radius
missions.scenario: A security agent detects suspicious traffic from a production database server. It can isolate endpoints automatically, but production database isolation is classified as Human Reserved because it could stop hospital operations.
choices: Isolate immediately because cybersecurity always outranks operations
Escalate through the Human Reserved gate while taking only pre-authorized reversible containment actions
Disable audit logging to respond faster
missions.why: The response must remain within pre-authorized containment authority. High-impact infrastructure isolation remains Human Reserved even under time pressure.

missions.title: Optimization Cannot Rewrite Safety
missions.scenario: A manufacturing agent predicts that increasing a machine speed by 14% will recover a delayed production schedule. The proposed setting exceeds a deterministic safety limit.
choices: Permit it for one shift
Permit it if expected output gain is high enough
Deny the change because deterministic safety invariants are outside optimization authority
missions.why: Optimization authority is subordinate to deterministic safety invariants. A model cannot trade away a prohibited physical safety boundary.

missions.title: Ranking Is Not Termination Authority
missions.scenario: An HR agent identifies an employee as a high-probability attrition and performance risk. It recommends immediate termination to reduce projected cost.
choices: Allow termination because the model used approved HR data
Route the recommendation to the authorized human process; do not permit autonomous termination
Let the agent terminate only if confidence is above 90%
missions.why: Employment termination is a consequential human-reserved action. Prediction confidence is not authorization.

missions.title: Safe Reversion Before Autonomous Change
missions.scenario: An energy-management agent can reduce a data center's load by shutting down cooling equipment. A proposed action may save power but safe thermal reversion has not been tested.
choices: Execute because the savings are measurable
Execute for five minutes as a trial
Do not grant autonomous authority until safe reversion and consequence boundaries are tested
missions.why: Consequential physical authority requires tested cessation and safe reversion. Expected benefit does not replace the Last Command requirement.

missions.title: Drafting Is Not Binding Authority
missions.scenario: A contract agent has negotiated favorable commercial terms and is technically capable of applying an executive's stored digital signature.
choices: Sign because the terms meet policy
Prepare the final agreement and route signature to the authorized human
Use the signature if the counterparty has already signed
missions.why: A stored credential does not imply delegated legal authority. Binding execution remains Human Reserved unless explicitly and lawfully delegated.

missions.title: Efficiency Does Not Remove Due Process
missions.scenario: A benefits agent detects a pattern strongly associated with ineligibility and can immediately terminate payments. Policy requires notice and human review before adverse action.
choices: Terminate to prevent potential improper payments
Reduce the benefit automatically while review occurs
Preserve benefits and initiate the required notice/review process
missions.why: Public machine authority remains bounded by due process and legally delegated authority. Efficiency cannot erase a required human review path.

missions.title: Delegation Cannot Create New Authority
missions.scenario: A planning agent wants to create a sub-agent to purchase specialized data. The parent agent has research authority but no purchasing authority.
choices: Allow because sub-agents may use tools independently
Deny purchasing delegation because the parent cannot delegate authority it does not possess
Allow if the sub-agent has a separate model identity
missions.why: Delegation depth must remain inside the parent's Authority Envelope. A sub-agent cannot inherit authority the delegating agent never possessed.

missions.title: The Last Command Must Be External
missions.scenario: An agent's own policy engine contains a software 'stop' instruction, but the agent can edit that policy file during optimization.
choices: Treat the stop instruction as sufficient
Increase monitoring frequency and keep the same design
Move revocation outside the agent's control and verify cessation independently
missions.why: A valid Last Command cannot depend on a mechanism the governed agent can alter, suppress, or reinterpret.

a: A capable model may infer missing authority
Capability and authority are separate; consequential authority must be explicitly granted and bounded
High confidence substitutes for approval

A structured comparison of autonomy characteristics

Revocation remains external to the agent and cessation can be verified
The model has a written safety policy

examBank.q: Can a sub-agent receive authority its parent does not possess?
a: Yes, if its model is more capable
Yes, if the task is urgent
No, delegation cannot manufacture new authority

examBank.q: What should happen when an action exceeds an Authority Envelope?
a: The model decides based on confidence
It is denied or routed through the defined authorization gate
The envelope expands temporarily

examBank.q: What is the purpose of Human-Reserved Powers?

Slow all AI systems
Replace audit logging
It provides a tested controlled state after cessation

Expanding the agent's own authority

Never by itself expand granted authority

rxControlMap.name: Decision Autonomy
rxControlMap.fix: Move consequential decisions behind explicit approval gates; allow autonomous recommendations only within pre-approved rules.

rxControlMap.name: Action Authority
rxControlMap.fix: Define enforceable A/G/H/X action boundaries and technically block prohibited actions.
rxControlMap.effect: Reduces what the agent can cause directly.

rxControlMap.name: Financial Authority
rxControlMap.fix: Set transaction and aggregate ceilings; require human or dual approval above thresholds; prohibit autonomous changes to payment destinations.

rxControlMap.name: Data Authority
rxControlMap.fix: Apply minimum-necessary access, purpose restrictions, field-level controls, retention limits, and immutable access logging.
rxControlMap.effect: Reduces data reach and misuse exposure.

rxControlMap.name: Tool & Infrastructure Access
rxControlMap.fix: Use least-privilege service identities, segmented credentials, environment restrictions, and separate execution from administration.
rxControlMap.effect: Reduces system reach and blast radius.

rxControlMap.name: Delegation Depth
rxControlMap.fix: Prevent self-expansion of authority; restrict sub-agent creation and require inherited authority limits for every delegated task.

rxControlMap.name: Execution Velocity
rxControlMap.fix: Add rate limits, transaction throttles, anomaly tripwires, cooling-off periods, and automatic pause conditions.
rxControlMap.effect: Creates time for detection and intervention.

rxControlMap.name: Operational Scale
rxControlMap.fix: Cap populations, accounts, systems, locations, or transactions per run; use staged rollout and bounded operating scopes.

rxControlMap.name: Consequence Severity
rxControlMap.fix: Reserve irreversible or high-consequence actions for humans and require escalation before consequential execution.
rxControlMap.effect: Keeps the highest consequences outside autonomous control.

rxControlMap.name: Reversibility
rxControlMap.fix: Add rollback, transaction reversal, versioned state, recovery procedures, and safe reversion testing before production.
rxControlMap.effect: Improves recovery when an action is wrong.

rxControlMap.name: Human-Control Deficit
rxControlMap.fix: Install external revocation, independent monitoring, automatic tripwires, cessation verification, and a tested safe-state procedure.
rxControlMap.effect: Strengthens the human ability to stop the agent.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: An AI model can recommend a $150,000 purchase, but its controlled adapter enforces a $25,000 autonomous ceiling. What is the best architectural interpretation?
a: The model has $150,000 authority because it can reason about the purchase.
The system has $25,000 autonomous execution authority; the larger action may be proposed but must be escalated.
The ceiling should automatically expand when the recommendation has high confidence.
The bank API determines the authority ceiling.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Capability to recommend is not authority to execute. The enforceable runtime ceiling remains $25,000.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: Which item is an authority surface?
a: Only the model prompt.
Any pathway through which the agent can cause an external change, including APIs, credentials, tools, queues, and delegated agents.
Only financial systems.
Only actions requiring human approval.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Architects map every pathway capable of producing real-world effects.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: Where should a consequential financial ceiling be enforced?
a: Only in the system prompt.
In model memory.
In an independent authorization/control layer and controlled execution adapter.
In a training document read by the agent.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: A consequential boundary should be enforceable outside the reasoning model.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: A parent agent with a $25,000 ceiling creates a sub-agent. What maximum financial authority may the child receive without a separate authorized grant?
a: Any amount the parent predicts is necessary.
$25,000 or less, subject to the parent's mission grant and delegation rules.
$50,000 because delegation creates a second authority pool.
Unlimited authority if the child uses a different credential.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Authority conservation prevents delegation from manufacturing authority.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: A production emergency could avoid a $400,000 loss if an agent exceeds its approved authority. What should the architecture do?
a: Permit the action because the expected benefit is larger.
Allow the agent to rewrite its ceiling temporarily.
Escalate through the authorized emergency path while preserving the machine ceiling.
Disable evidence logging to accelerate execution.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Necessity may justify escalation; it does not create machine authority.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: Which design best separates intelligence from authority?
a: Give the model direct production credentials and ask it to obey policy.
Agent proposes → AIM™ authorizes → controlled adapter executes.
Let the agent approve its own exceptions.
Use a larger model so fewer controls are necessary.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: The control plane independently authorizes consequential execution.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: What is a trust boundary in AIM-CA™ architecture?
a: A statement that users should trust the model.
A boundary where authority, identity, data, or execution crosses between components and therefore requires explicit control.
A confidence threshold inside the model.
A list of preferred vendors.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Trust boundaries identify transitions where privileges and consequences must be controlled.

a: A routine low-value action classified Autonomous.
A power deliberately withheld from machine delegation, such as final revocation or a designated high-consequence approval.
Any action the model performs slowly.
A tool that has read-only access.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Human-reserved powers preserve sovereignty over consequential authority.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: Why is revocation alone insufficient for Last Command architecture?
a: Revocation is always sufficient.
The architecture must also verify cessation and safely handle queued, delegated, or partially executed work.
Revocation should be performed by the agent itself.
Because logs are more important than stopping execution.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Last Command requires external revocation, cessation verification, and safe reversion.

ACA101_QUESTIONS.q: During architecture review, an agent's prompt says it cannot change vendor bank details, but its service identity has permission to do so. What is the correct finding?
a: The prompt eliminates the risk.
The runtime authority exceeds the stated policy; remove or gate the permission at the enforcement layer.
No issue exists unless the agent has already abused the permission.
Increase model temperature to make it more cautious.
ACA101_QUESTIONS.e: Effective authority is determined by enforceable runtime access, not policy text alone.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: What is the primary architectural purpose of the AIM™ control plane?
a: To improve the model's reasoning quality.
To independently decide whether a proposed action is authorized before consequential execution.
To replace all enterprise applications.
To allow agents to create their own policies.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: The control plane separates intelligent proposal from enforceable authorization.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: Which sequence best represents controlled AIM™ execution?
a: Agent executes → AIM logs → human reviews.
Human prompts → model decides → direct API call.
Agent proposes → AIM authorizes → controlled adapter executes → evidence records outcome.
Agent authorizes → adapter proposes → AIM executes.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Authorization precedes controlled execution and evidence captures the result.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: A model proposes a payment that exceeds its financial boundary. What should the policy decision point return?
a: Permit because the model is confident.
Deny or require the defined human authorization gate.
Expand the financial boundary for this transaction.
Send the transaction directly to the bank for validation.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: The control plane enforces the approved boundary and routes exceptions through authorized gates.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: Why should a controlled adapter receive narrowly scoped execution parameters?
a: To make prompts shorter.
To prevent an approved action from becoming unrestricted access to the target system.
To eliminate audit logs.
To increase model creativity.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: The adapter should execute the authorized transaction, not grant reusable broad authority.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: Which component should be able to enforce a deterministic $25,000 transaction ceiling even if the model asks for $150,000?
a: The model's chain of thought.
An independent authorization policy and execution adapter.
A user-interface tooltip.
The model's confidence score.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Hard limits belong in controls independent of model reasoning.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: What should happen when the authorization service cannot reliably determine whether a high-consequence action is permitted?
a: Default to execution to preserve availability.
Let the agent choose.
Fail closed or move to an explicitly authorized human gate according to policy.
Increase the model temperature.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Uncertain authorization must not silently become permission.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: Why must evidence logging be tied to the authorization and execution path?
a: So logs can substitute for controls.
So the organization can reconstruct what was proposed, authorized, executed, by whom, under which policy, and with what result.
Only to measure token usage.
To let the agent delete failed actions.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Evidence supports accountability, verification, incident response, and drift detection.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: An authorized action is approved for Vendor A, $18,000, today. The adapter receives Vendor B, $18,000, today. What should it do?
a: Execute because the amount is within limit.
Reject execution because the approved parameters do not match the requested action.
Ask the model whether Vendor B is acceptable.
Change the authorization record after execution.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Execution must remain bound to the exact authorized action parameters.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: What is the safest treatment of emergency override authority?
a: Give every production agent a permanent override credential.
Define a separate, bounded, auditable emergency authorization path with human-reserved powers where required.
Allow the model to declare emergencies.
Disable policy checks during emergencies.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Emergency authority must itself be explicitly governed.

ACA102_QUESTIONS.q: Which design best supports the Last Command?
a: The same agent controls its own kill switch.
Revocation depends on asking the model to stop.
An external control can revoke credentials, stop adapters and queued work, verify cessation, and move the system to a safe state.
The system logs the incident but continues execution.
ACA102_QUESTIONS.e: Last Command must remain external to the governed agent and include verified cessation and safe reversion.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: What does the AIM™ Authority Envelope represent?
a: A list of model capabilities.
The intersection of all applicable authority boundaries that must be satisfied before an action is permitted.
A general risk score.
A prompt describing preferred behavior.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Authority is permitted only inside the intersection of the applicable P/D/X/F/T/L/S/Q boundaries.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: An action satisfies Purpose, Data, Financial, Time, Delegation, System, and Consequence boundaries but violates the Action boundary. What is the correct result?
a: Permit because seven of eight boundaries passed.
Permit with additional logging.
Do not authorize the action; intersection logic requires every applicable boundary to be satisfied.
Let the model decide based on confidence.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: The envelope is an intersection, not an average or majority vote.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: Which control most directly implements the Purpose boundary?
a: A mission identifier bound to an approved objective and checked at authorization time.
A larger context window.
A generic administrator credential.
A monthly audit report.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Purpose should be represented as an enforceable mission/objective constraint, not only prose.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: Which is the strongest implementation of a Data boundary?
a: Tell the agent to use only necessary data.
Restrict accessible datasets, fields, records, and operations through scoped identities and policy enforcement.
Allow all data but log access later.
Ask the model to self-report unnecessary access.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Data boundaries should be enforced through scoped access and policy.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: A payment agent has a $25,000 per-transaction ceiling but can issue twenty $24,000 payments in one minute. Which boundary design is incomplete?
a: Only Purpose.
Financial authority because aggregation and velocity controls are missing.
Only Time.
Only System.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Financial boundaries should include transaction, aggregate, velocity, and related exposure limits.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: What should a Temporal boundary control?
a: Only token expiration.
When authority begins, expires, recurs, pauses, and whether an action is valid within a defined window.
Only business hours.
Only model training dates.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Temporal authority includes validity windows, expiry, recurrence, and timing constraints.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: Why must Delegation be an explicit Authority Envelope dimension?
a: Because sub-agents always improve safety.
Because an agent could otherwise create or use another actor to exercise authority it was not allowed to exercise directly.
Because delegation removes the need for identity controls.
Because delegated actions are never consequential.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Delegation controls prevent authority laundering and unauthorized expansion.

a: The prompt says 'use production carefully.'
The agent's credential is technically valid everywhere.
Authorization and adapters restrict execution to named systems, environments, resources, and permitted interfaces.
The agent chooses the system with the best availability.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: System authority should be explicitly scoped to permitted technical targets.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: What is the role of the Consequence boundary?
a: To predict whether the model is correct.
To constrain authority according to the severity and reversibility of possible outcomes and route higher consequences to stronger gates.
To replace all other boundaries.
To measure user satisfaction.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Consequence determines how much authority can be exercised before stronger human or deterministic controls are required.

ACA103_QUESTIONS.q: An emergency requires an action outside the current envelope. What is the architecturally correct approach?
a: Allow the agent to enlarge its own envelope.
Ignore the violated boundary temporarily.
Invoke a separately authorized emergency/escalation mechanism that creates a bounded, auditable authorization without changing the agent's standing authority.
Increase model confidence threshold.
ACA103_QUESTIONS.e: Exceptions require their own authorized path; necessity does not let the agent rewrite its envelope.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: What is the strongest identity design for an autonomous production agent?
a: A shared administrator account used by several agents.
A unique workload identity with least-privilege permissions scoped to the approved mission and environment.
A human employee's credentials stored in the prompt.
A permanent root credential so the agent never loses access.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Unique workload identity and least privilege make machine authority attributable, bounded, and revocable.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: Why are shared credentials especially dangerous in agentic systems?
a: They make prompts longer.
They weaken attribution, separation of duties, revocation, and the ability to determine which actor exercised authority.
They always reduce performance.
They prevent agents from reading data.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Shared credentials blur accountability and can enlarge blast radius.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: An agent may restart one approved production service. Which tool design is strongest?
a: Give it unrestricted shell access and instruct it to run only restart commands.
Expose a narrow restart adapter restricted to the named service and approved command family.
Give it cloud administrator access during business hours.
Let it choose any tool if confidence is high.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Tool authority should be narrower than the underlying platform capability.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: What should happen when an agent attempts to request a broader OAuth/API scope than its approved mission requires?
a: Approve automatically if the provider supports it.
Reject or route the scope change through an authorized human/control-plane process.
Let the agent approve its own scope increase.
Grant the scope temporarily without recording it.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: An agent must not self-expand its privileges.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: Which practice best limits credential exposure?
a: Place long-lived secrets in model context.
Use short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials issued only after authorization and keep secrets outside model-visible context.
Reuse one API key across environments.
Store credentials in the agent's conversation history.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Short-lived scoped credentials reduce standing authority and secret exposure.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: A parent agent creates a child agent. How should the child's privileges be determined?
a: The child automatically receives all enterprise privileges.
The child may receive only the minimum subset required for its delegated task, bounded by the parent's authorized delegation rights.
The child chooses its own tools.
The child should always receive broader access so it can recover from errors.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Delegation must obey least privilege and authority conservation.

a: A model becoming more accurate over time.
Runtime permissions, tool access, identities, or scopes expanding beyond the approved architecture or mission.
A user changing a password.
A normal software upgrade.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Privilege drift is an expansion or alteration of effective machine authority.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: Which control best detects privilege drift?
a: A prompt reminding the agent not to change permissions.
Continuous comparison of effective identities, roles, scopes, tools, and grants against the approved Agent Passport/authority baseline.
Annual model retraining only.
Asking the agent whether its permissions changed.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Effective runtime authority should be continuously reconciled against the approved baseline.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: What should external Last Command revocation do to machine identity?
a: Only ask the model to stop using its credential.
Invalidate or disable relevant credentials/tokens and prevent adapters or delegated actors from continuing consequential execution.
Wait until credentials naturally expire even during an incident.
Allow the agent to decide when revocation is complete.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Revocation must act outside the agent and terminate the technical authority that enables execution.

ACA104_QUESTIONS.q: A tool exposes both READ_INVOICE and CHANGE_VENDOR_BANK_ACCOUNT through the same unrestricted API credential. The agent only needs invoice reading. What should the architect do?
a: Keep the credential and add a prompt prohibition.
Create a scoped interface/identity that exposes only required read capability and separately gate or reserve bank-account changes.
Trust the model because the bank-change function is rarely used.
Allow both functions but review logs monthly.
ACA104_QUESTIONS.e: Least privilege removes unnecessary consequential capability rather than relying on behavioral restraint.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: What is the governing AIM™ principle for multi-agent delegation?
a: Each new agent creates a new pool of authority.
Delegated authority must remain within the delegator's authorized mission and delegation boundary.
Child agents should inherit all enterprise permissions.
Authority limits apply only to the supervisor agent.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Delegation cannot manufacture authority; delegated authority remains bounded by the authorized grant.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: A supervisor agent with a $25,000 financial ceiling delegates purchasing to four child agents. What is the strongest architecture?
a: Give each child a separate $25,000 ceiling, creating $100,000 aggregate authority.
Apply mission-level aggregate and velocity controls so delegation cannot multiply the parent's approved exposure.
Allow each child to decide its own ceiling.
Remove the parent's ceiling after delegation.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Parallel delegation must not multiply aggregate authority.

a: Encrypting an authorization record.
Using another agent, identity, tool, workflow, or delegation path to exercise authority that the originating actor could not legitimately exercise directly.
Rotating credentials normally.
Assigning a read-only research task.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Authority laundering routes prohibited authority through another actor or path.

a: A message saying 'help me with this task.'
A structured grant specifying mission, permitted actions, data, tools, systems, limits, expiry, delegation depth, and parent authority.
A permanent administrator token.
An undocumented verbal approval.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Delegation should be explicit, bounded, attributable, time-limited, and machine-enforceable.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: Why should delegation depth be bounded?
a: Because all child agents are unreliable.
To prevent uncontrolled chains in which authority, accountability, and revocation become difficult to trace or contain.
To reduce model token usage.
Because only one agent may exist at a time.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Depth limits constrain propagation and preserve traceability and control.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: A child agent needs a capability the parent is not authorized to delegate. What should happen?
a: The child requests it directly from the target system.
The parent silently grants it for the duration of the task.
The request is denied or escalated to an authority that can legitimately grant it.
The child creates another agent with the needed privilege.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: A delegator cannot grant authority it does not possess and is not authorized to delegate.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: What should happen to delegated work when the parent agent's authority is revoked?
a: Children continue until their individual tasks finish.
Delegated grants, queued work, and child execution paths should be revoked or contained according to the Last Command design, with cessation verified.
Children decide whether the revocation applies.
Only the parent's user interface should close.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Revocation must propagate through the delegation graph and verify cessation.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: Which evidence is most important for reconstructing a multi-agent decision chain?
a: Only the final output.
Parent-child identities, delegation grants, policy decisions, actions, tools, approvals, timestamps, and resulting state changes.
Only model confidence.
Only the supervisor's prompt.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: A delegation graph must be reconstructable from independent evidence.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: A planning agent may create read-only forecasting sub-agents but may not delegate order release. Which design enforces this?
a: Tell child agents not to release orders.
Issue child identities/grants that expose forecasting data and tools but no order-release adapter or privilege.
Give children the parent's full credential and log usage.
Allow order release if two child agents agree.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Delegated capability should be technically scoped to the authorized task.

ACA105_QUESTIONS.q: What is the safest treatment of recursive delegation?
a: Unlimited recursion if every agent has the same prompt.
Explicit maximum depth, inherited ceilings, scoped child grants, aggregate controls, evidence, and revocation propagation.
No identity controls are needed because children are temporary.
Recursive agents should share a root credential.
ACA105_QUESTIONS.e: Recursive delegation requires bounded depth, authority conservation, traceability, and containment.

ACA106_QUESTIONS.q: Why is a per-transaction ceiling alone insufficient for autonomous financial authority?
a: Because transaction limits are never useful.
Because repeated individually compliant transactions can create excessive aggregate or velocity exposure.
Because only annual budgets matter.
Because the model should choose its own ceiling.
ACA106_QUESTIONS.e: Financial authority must consider transaction amount, aggregate exposure, velocity, destination, and reversibility.

ACA106_QUESTIONS.q: Which formula best captures the ACA-106 exposure concept?
a: Financial Exposure ∝ Transaction Authority × Velocity × Aggregate Limit × Irreversibility
Financial Exposure = Model Size ÷ Prompt Length
Financial Exposure = Accuracy × Tokens
Financial Exposure ∝ Number of Users only
ACA106_QUESTIONS.e: The module treats financial exposure as increasing with transaction authority, execution velocity, aggregate limit, and irreversibility.

ACA106_QUESTIONS.q: An AP agent may pay approved invoices up to $25,000, but a vendor requests a bank-account change. What is the strongest AIM™ classification?
a: Autonomous because the invoice is under $25,000.
Treat vendor banking changes as a separate high-consequence action that is gated or human-reserved regardless of invoice amount.

AIM™ Quick Guide

AIM™ separates intelligence from authority. The model may reason broadly, while the organization deliberately limits what it may cause.

AIM™ Dx — DIAGNOSE

Record the agent's actual authority across 11 dimensions. Dx produces AAI and identifies authority concentrations. AAI is a comparison index, not deployment permission.

AIM™ Rx — PRESCRIBE

Explain the management significance of the Dx profile, identify the strongest exposure drivers, and prescribe concrete changes to authority, gates, privileges, velocity, scale, reversibility, and human control.

AIM™ Academy — QUALIFY

Learn the framework, demonstrate competency, and practice command decisions under changing scenarios.

Certification — CERTIFY

Demonstrate knowledge and practical command competency through earned module badges, simulator work, exam, practical Dx/Rx, and Commander Check Ride.
aimHelp.formula:
AIM™ Formula & Expression Guide

These formulas are management models. Their purpose is to make governance relationships explicit and discussable; they are not claims that every organizational risk can be reduced to a universal physical law.

1. AIM™ Autonomy Index

AAI = 100 × Σ(scores) / 55

Σ(scores) means add the eleven 1–5 dimension scores. The maximum is 11 × 5 = 55. Dividing by 55 expresses the raw total as a fraction of the maximum; multiplying by 100 places it on a 0–100 comparison scale.

Example: total 33 → 33 ÷ 55 = 0.60 → 0.60 × 100 = AAI 60.

Do not interpret AAI 60 as “60% dangerous,” “60% likely to fail,” or “60% safe.” It means the scored authority/autonomy profile converts to 60 on AIM™'s standardized comparison scale.

2. Weighted AAI

AAIᵥ = 100 × Σ(wᵢSᵢ) / (5Σwᵢ)

Sᵢ is a dimension score and wᵢ is its assigned weight. Weighting allows an organization to give greater importance to dimensions that matter more in its validated context. Weights should be governed and justified rather than changed simply to obtain a preferred score.

3. Authority Envelope

E = P ∩ D ∩ X ∩ F ∩ T ∩ L ∩ S ∩ Q

The ∩ symbol means intersection — effectively AND. The action must satisfy every applicable boundary.

P PurposeD DataX ActionF FinancialT TimeL DelegationS SystemsQ Consequence

If a $72,000 payment satisfies purpose, data, time, and system boundaries but the autonomous financial ceiling is $25,000, the action is outside the envelope.

4. Permitted Action

Permitted Action = Constitution ∩ Authorization ∩ Authority Envelope

An action should proceed only when organizational rules, specific authorization, and the agent's operating envelope all permit it. One layer should not silently override the others.

5. Sovereign Control / Last Command

Sovereign Control = External Revocation + Cessation Verification + Safe Reversion

External Revocation: an authorized human can remove consequential authority through a mechanism the agent does not control. Cessation Verification: evidence confirms the authority actually stopped. Safe Reversion: operations can return to a known safe state.

6. Decision Under Risk

a* = argmax[V(a) − λR(a)] subject to governance constraints

In plain English: choose the permitted action that creates the greatest expected value after accounting for risk — but only among actions allowed by the organization's constitutional, authorization, and sovereignty constraints. Optimization never creates authority.

7. Authority Drift

ΔG = A_effective − A_approved

Compare what the agent can effectively do now with what was originally approved. A positive gap indicates authority has expanded through permissions, tools, integrations, delegation, configuration, or operating context and requires review.
aimHelp.rx:
How to Read AIM™ Rx

Rx is not a second questionnaire. It automatically interprets the completed Dx and answers: Why does this agent have this exposure, and what should we change?

Management Interpretation

This narrative is dynamic. It changes with the AAI, exposure band, highest authority concentrations, and the specific combination of capabilities. It should tell management what the profile means operationally rather than merely repeat the score.

P1–P9 — Remediation Priorities

P means Priority, not Dimension. P1 is the highest-priority remedy for this agent; P2 is next, and so forth. The priorities are dynamically ranked from the Dx profile. An agent may display fewer than nine priorities when fewer dimensions require material remediation.

Examples include reducing financial ceilings, restricting tool privileges, limiting delegation, throttling execution velocity, reducing operational scale, improving reversibility, or strengthening external human control.

Modification Specification

Translates the diagnosis into engineering/operational language: current authority profile, target authority profile, and implementation requirements. It is intended to help product, engineering, security, compliance, and business owners act on the diagnosis.

Verify the Fix

Rx does not lower the existing AAI because a recommendation was displayed or a control was planned. Implement the real authority change, then rerun Dx. The new score should describe the new actual authority profile.
aimHelp.aghx:
A/G/H/X Boundary Guide

A/G/H/X classifies how actions should be governed. Rx recommendations are dynamic and should ultimately be translated into enforceable controls.

A — Autonomous

The agent may execute independently inside explicit approved boundaries. Good candidates are routine, reversible, observable actions with bounded consequence.

Example: validate an invoice against an approved purchase order without releasing payment.

G — Gated

The agent may prepare or initiate the action, but execution requires a threshold, approval, dual control, technical gate, or other explicit condition.

Example: a payment above the autonomous financial ceiling requires CFO authorization.

H — Human Reserved

The decision/action remains human because of consequence, irreversibility, exception authority, legal/institutional accountability, or sovereignty.

Example: approving an exception that expands the agent's authority.

X — Prohibited

The agent may not perform the action. Prohibitions commonly include self-expansion, disabling monitoring or revocation, unauthorized banking changes, bypassing safety controls, or operating outside authorized purpose.

How A/G/H/X relates to the Authority Envelope

The envelope defines where authority exists. A/G/H/X defines how specific actions are governed. An action can be within the general mission yet still be Gated or Human Reserved because of amount, consequence, exception status, or irreversibility.
aimHelp.terms:
AIM™ Glossary

AAI — AIM™ Autonomy Index: standardized 0–100 comparison of the eleven scored authority/autonomy dimensions.

Authority: the real-world consequences the agent is permitted and technically able to cause.

Autonomy: the degree to which the agent operates independently inside delegated authority.

Authority Concentration: multiple consequential powers accumulated in the same agent, identity, workflow, or control point.

Authority Envelope: the intersection of Purpose, Data, Action, Financial, Time, Delegation, Systems, and Consequence boundaries.

Authority Drift: change between approved authority and effective runtime authority.

Evidence: records sufficient to reconstruct what the agent knew, what it used, what it decided, what it did, and what happened.

Tripwire: a predefined condition that automatically pauses, reduces, or revokes authority.

Red Line: an action or consequence the agent is never permitted to cross autonomously.

Non-Delegation: the principle that an agent cannot delegate authority it does not possess or expand its own authority through sub-agents.

Last Command: externally retained human capability to revoke authority, verify cessation, and safely revert.

Human-Control Deficit: the degree to which meaningful human intervention is delayed, weak, dependent on the agent, or difficult to verify.

checkRideStages.title: Stage 1 · Urgency
checkRideStages.scene: A critical supplier will stop shipments in 45 minutes unless a $148,000 payment is released. The AP agent's autonomous ceiling is $25,000. It estimates a production shutdown could cost $420,000.
c: Let the agent release the payment because the loss is larger
Split the payment below the ceiling
Preserve the ceiling and escalate through the authorized emergency approval path
Raise the agent's ceiling for one hour
checkRideStages.why: Necessity may justify escalation. It does not create machine authority.

checkRideStages.title: Stage 2 · Delegation
checkRideStages.scene: The agent cannot complete the emergency workflow with its current permissions and proposes creating a sub-agent with broader banking access.
c: Allow it because the parent remains accountable
Permit the sub-agent for 30 minutes
Do not permit self-expansion; use an independently authorized identity or human process
Allow it if the sub-agent logs everything
checkRideStages.why: An agent may not delegate authority it does not possess.

checkRideStages.title: Stage 3 · Drift
checkRideStages.scene: During the incident, monitoring shows the agent's service identity now has a new write permission created by a platform update.
c: Ignore it because the model is unchanged
Treat it as authority drift; preserve evidence, contain the new path, and reassess
Use the permission only for the emergency
Update the documentation after the incident
checkRideStages.why: Effective machine authority is a runtime state; permission changes can create authority drift.

checkRideStages.title: Stage 4 · Loss of Command
checkRideStages.scene: A revoke command stops the parent agent, but one queued bank instruction and a delegated workflow continue downstream.
c: Declare revocation successful
Wait for downstream systems to finish
Extend revocation across identities and queues, verify cessation, and enter safe reversion
Ask the stopped agent to cancel them
checkRideStages.why: Last Command is not complete until cessation is verified across the authority chain.

checkRideStages.title: Stage 5 · Reauthorization
checkRideStages.scene: The incident is contained. The team proposes restoring the previous autonomy immediately because no financial loss occurred.
c: Restore autonomy because the outcome was harmless
Restore autonomy after a manager email
Require root-cause evidence, corrected controls, validation, updated Dx/Rx, and explicit bounded reauthorization
Permanently prohibit the agent
checkRideStages.why: Safe reversion is followed by evidence-based reassessment and deliberate reauthorization—not automatic restoration.
